Today's second meeting
National Assembly
(1:43 PM)
Honorable Members,
Chairperson: Honorable Members, the proceedings of the meeting commence now. I would like to provide time to the Honorable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle to present the proposal for consideration of the "Appropriation Bill, 2083" received with a message from the House of Representatives.
Honorable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle: Honorable Members,
(1:43 PM)
Mr. Speaker, Sir, with the permission of the Speaker, I present before this esteemed assembly the proposal for consideration of the "Appropriation Bill, 2083" received with a message from the House of Representatives. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Members, the discussion on the proposal for consideration of the "Appropriation Bill, 2083" received with a message from the House of Representatives commences. I would like to inform you that only the theoretical aspect of the bill will be discussed in this process. I request the Honorable Members who wish to participate in the discussion to submit their names within two minutes. I have allocated three minutes to each Honorable Member participating in the discussion. First, Honorable Member Padam Bahadur Pariyar.
Honorable Mr. Padam Bahadur Pariyar (Nepali Congress): Honorable Mr. Speaker, Sir,
(1:45 PM)
While discussing, I would like to draw the attention of the Honorable Minister to two specific issues. Especially regarding the inter-governmental fiscal transfer system that has been arranged. In this bill, there is a provision to transfer funds to local levels and provinces by setting a deadline first, but later there is a provision to transfer funds based on revenue collected. This will make it very difficult for local levels and provinces to estimate things they have already included in their budgets and to implement programs they have already planned. Therefore, I feel that clause 6, sub-clause (4) needs to be reconsidered.
Honorable Mr. Speaker, Sir, another issue is that the provision written in clause 10, sub-clause (3), which states that "appropriation shall not be considered contrary to law," is very ambiguous. It is arranged in such a way that even if it is contrary to any law, if it has already been included in the budget book, it will not be considered an appropriation contrary to law. Now, it is possible that we have not understood this, but it seems that the legislature has given too much flexibility to the executive. And finally, regarding schedule 1, which has been in place for many years. I am specifically talking about the budget allocated to commissions like the Dalit Commission, Women's Commission, etc. It appears that the government has allocated budgets only for basic functioning. I had expected that the Honorable Minister would change this trend. It was also a high priority in the policy and program, but this time the budget for these constitutional commissions has not increased. I want to be clear on these issues, thank you.
Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Madan Kumari Shah "Garima".
(1:48 PM)
Honorable Mr. Madan Kumari Shah "Garima" (Communist Party of Nepal (UML)):
(1:48 PM)
Honorable Mr. Speaker, Sir, today we are discussing the Appropriation Bill. While the budget statement is a proposal on what the government will do and how much it will spend, the Appropriation Bill is the legal permission to spend the budget proposed by the government. This bill specifies which ministry or body will be legally authorized to spend how much amount under which head. Parliament grants this authority to the government to facilitate its functioning, but there have been instances of misuse of the authority granted by Parliament. It has been reintroduced with provisions to make necessary arrangements to fulfill political objectives, giving the Council of Ministers the authority of Parliament. Theoretically, this provision needs to be discussed. The budget passed by Parliament is cut or postponed based on political vendettas without even informing Parliament, and finally, funds are transferred to desired places. A glaring example is the extensive reduction of plans passed by the previous government, which were recommended by Parliament.
Honorable Mr. Speaker, Sir, in response to the questions and queries raised on the budget statement, the Honorable Minister had said that expanding the middle class means raising the poor to expand the middle class. I was optimistic. I thought the budget allocation would come in that way, but looking at this budget allocation, it is neither for the middle class nor for the poor. The state's duty to ensure social justice seems to have been completely forgotten in this budget allocation. The increase in taxes on basic services like education, health, and electricity will start a new cycle of inflation, which will burden the middle class. The poor will fall deeper into the clutches of poverty. The budget seems to be designed to oppress the middle class and impoverish the poor. The budget of the Government of Nepal is full of ambitious thoughts and declarations, but there is no plan on how to develop the implementation capacity. Through the Honorable Mr. Speaker, Sir, I want to tell the Honorable Minister that the success of the government, i.e., the budget, depends not on thought, but on the basis of data. The budget has been presented in such a way that it is based on borrowing to repay principal and interest. Reliability is also a basis for implementation, but questions have arisen about reliability due to changes in tax rates within two days of the budget's public release. Transferring funds from capital expenditure to current expenditure is a violation of the law. There seems to be no coordination between the Ministry of Finance and the National Planning Commission.
Honorable Mr. Speaker, Sir, the government's budget is not a neutral document; it is a reflection of class relations. It is about whether it favors laborers, farmers, and the poor, or the rich capitalists. The budget allocation is not transformative in terms of production relations; it is status quoist. The budget claims to create employment but does not focus on workers' wages, trade union rights, social security expansion, and worker participation in production. Poverty is not just due to a lack of income; it is due to inequality in production relations. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Roshni Mechhe.
(1:51 PM)
Honorable Mr. Roshni Mechhe (Nepal Communist Party (UML)): Honorable Mr. Speaker, Sir,
(1:51 PM)
We are in the theoretical discussion of this Appropriation Bill. I seek permission to raise a few points, two or three points. Now, regarding how this Appropriation Bill will be implemented, a process of seeking permission from Parliament has been completed with the presentation of this Appropriation Bill in Parliament. Beyond that, there has been a significant change in the tax rates or the creation of new taxes. This has created a discouraging environment for entrepreneurs, businessmen, and investors. This is because one type of provision was made in the Appropriation Bill, and then the government changed the tax rates outside of it, so how will the industrialists and businessmen proceed? They will be afraid. The government makes one arrangement in an Appropriation Bill and then adds something else. This has created fear and discouragement among industrialists and businessmen. This is a theoretical issue.
Another issue is that there appears to be ample deposits in banks, but there is uncertainty about how the government will invest this. To create a good environment by flowing more loans, it seems the government has faltered a bit in this regard.
I would like to emphasize the issue of strengthening federalism. We have three tiers of government: local, provincial, and federal. Regarding the budget allocation, in the previous fiscal year, the budget allocation seemed somewhat equitable, but in the current budget, it appears that less amount has been allocated, rather than strengthening federalism.
Another theoretical point is that we always expect that after a new government comes, the budget will be managed in a new way. The center should make the budget by asking the provincial government, or the province should ask the local level, but this government seems to have faltered again. When the center imposes a budget that is different from the needs of the local level, we face implementation problems, and again this government has brought a similar budget, which is theoretically very inconsistent and poses implementation challenges. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Narayan Dutt Mishra.
(1:54 PM)
Honorable Mr. Narayan Dutt Mishra (Nepali Congress): Honorable Mr. Speaker, Sir,
(1:54 PM)
We participate in the theoretical discussion of the Appropriation Bill every year. Sometimes we criticize, and sometimes we express support. The face of the budget is always the same. Sometimes it's painted with one color, and sometimes with another. I would like to give this bill the status of a directionless bill. The budget aims to spend a lot, but it has not provided a reliable basis for achieving results. On one hand, the revenue base is weakening, and on the other hand, the size of expenditure is unnecessarily increasing. An ambitious budget with an uncertain source of funding can lead to financial risks rather than maintaining financial discipline.
The problem of capital expenditure is perennial. There is no novelty. Funds are allocated, but the pace and progress of construction remain the same. The main reason seems to be a lack of accountability in implementation. On one hand, it is claimed that job creation and production growth are prioritized, while on the other hand, there is no clear strategy. Young people are increasingly forced to go abroad. There is a lack of concrete basis for transforming agriculture, industry, and tourism; it is left to God. The spirit of federalism has been completely disregarded. There is neither a plan nor a vision to empower provincial and local levels. Equitable distribution of maximum resources is necessary. There is a fear that good governance and the effectiveness of public spending will be weakened due to irregularities, delays, and weak discipline. We are ready to cooperate positively with the Parliament, and we are ready to cooperate positively with the government. The Nepali Congress's policy has never been to oppose for the sake of opposition, nor will it be in the future. We want the expenditure to be as much as possible and to be a reflection of the change in people's lives. The budget should not be a book of popular declarations; it should be an action plan that delivers results. With such expectations, we humbly request the government to correct these weaknesses in the theoretical basis of the presented Appropriation Bill and draw its attention. While the theoretical discussion of the Appropriation Bill continues as a new version of an old story, political theories worldwide have become outdated, and democracy and populism have overshadowed theory.

has taken place. The principle of the allocated budget states that every year there should be all-round development of the country, but the budget management always chooses favoritism. Sudurpashchim, Karnali, and Madhesh always have to endure step-motherly treatment. This has been going on since the Rana period (.... time is up| ).

Honorable Chairperson: Honorable member Somnath Purtal.
(14:58 hrs)
Honorable Mr. Somnath Purtal (Nepal Communist Party, UML):- Honorable
(14:58 hrs)
Chairperson, I seek permission to briefly present my views on the theoretical discussion of the Appropriation Bill. We have primarily moved towards federalism to develop our own regions, our own areas, and to increase public participation in development, and constitutional and legal provisions were made to develop local governments as strong governments.
For that, local levels and provinces need to be empowered and strengthened with resources, means, and manpower, but looking at the Appropriation Bill through the government's budget, it is seen that the amount of grants going to local levels and provinces is decreasing every year, the percentage is decreasing. Looking at last year's data, it is seen that last year 5.54 percent grant went to the local level, this year it is 5.11 percent, a significant amount, a big figure. If the grants going to local levels and provinces continue to decrease in this way, if the resources continue to decrease, are we strengthening federalism or weakening it? This is a serious question. Therefore, while appropriating, it seems to me that we should move in a direction where more goes to the local level and it should be gradually increased. Second, looking at this appropriation, it is seen that even small programs, especially those that can be handled by the ward, are kept in the ministry. Even programs that can be done by the ward are kept in the ministry of the federal government. If this is done, I don't think it will move in the direction of effective implementation plans as it should be.
Third, we have done revenue sharing, and it is proposed in the Appropriation Bill that 12 percent of the total revenue will be shared with local levels and provinces, it is mentioned in the Appropriation Bill. If a large portion of revenue remains in the center, and a large portion of all resources remains in the center, how will the work done by the local level and provincial level be effective? A clear question has arisen. If resources are not provided, and hands are tied, and then local levels and provinces are deemed useless, it is not enough to just give them blame. Local levels and provinces must be empowered and strengthened with resources, means, and manpower. I urge that the Appropriation Bill should pay attention to that direction. Thank you.

Honorable Chairperson: And
Honorable member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota.
(15:01 hrs)
Honorable Ms. Bishnu Kumari Sapkota (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson,
(15:01 hrs)
We are going into the theoretical discussion of this budget, the Appropriation Budget. Looking at the budget superficially, the budget seemed very good when reading it. But looking at this budget in depth, its sources are not visible.
Local levels, local governments, must be made the strongest. In the budget of 2082/2083, the equalization grant for the local level was cut in its last installment. When that installment was cut, it was very difficult for the local level to do many things, and when it came again, the equalization grant has been reduced again, and there have been changes in revenue sharing as well. Because of this, I don't think this budget has been kept in a good GRB logic, and even for agriculture, which is the most important for us, the budget allocated and the programs that should have been there are not seen. Agriculture should be taken as the basis. I would like to request through the Honorable Chairperson to correct things like imposing taxes on education and health. Thank you.

Honorable Chairperson: Honorable members, the message received from the House of Representatives
(15:03 hrs)
"Appropriation Bill, 2080" is for consideration. The discussion by honorable members will conclude here. Honorable members, I now provide time to the Honorable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle to respond to the questions raised in the discussion.

Honorable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle:- Honorable Chairperson, we
(15:03 hrs)
consider the National Assembly with special importance. We also consider it as a forum for debate in many places, and we come with expectations that we will receive diverse ideas, feedback, and advanced suggestions on matters of statecraft, which are different from the atmosphere of the House of Representatives. Therefore, I am happy to be present in the National Assembly today and to hear your views. Issues have been raised. Now, I have already responded to some of the points we raised after the budget statement. Nevertheless, since the honorable members have reiterated their queries, I wish to respond to them as well.
First, regarding the issue of intergovernmental fiscal transfer raised by Honorable Padam Pariyar, whether it will be difficult to plan at the local level if revenue is not received as expected. This is reasonable, but we cannot raise loans for money that has not been raised and then reduce the center to give to the local level. Therefore, after it is written in the Appropriation Bill beforehand, the local level also has to proceed according to the principle of anticipatory planning, realizing that if revenue is not collected as targeted, both the top and the bottom will shrink. Now, if everyone collects revenue as per the target, how much will go down is determined by formula according to the constitution. These matters are also directed by the Finance Commission. Therefore, 15 percent VAT and 15 percent excise duty go to the provinces and local levels. This time too, while setting a target of 1480 billion, we have set targets to send about 175 billion down for revenue sharing. Our sincere effort will be for everyone to collect revenue as per the target and to allocate funds downwards as per the formula determined by the constitution. But if the revenue is not collected as targeted, both the top and the bottom will shrink. We have to move forward according to the principle of partnership.
There is a question about whether Article 10 has delegated too much authority. Now, in all these functioning democracies, in the Westminster system of democracy, this is the system. The parliament sets a limit. The validity of a fundamental delegation is given by the parliament, the National Assembly, the House of Representatives. We present our targets to the parliament. We will spend this much. These are the estimated targets of resources. This much from foreign loans, this much from our internal revenue, this much from foreign grants, we set these targets. But the responsibility of doing the nitty-gritty, detailed work within that lies with the executive, so if the parliament starts coming for every small program, we cannot work. Therefore, we work according to the principle of delegated authority. But the parliament itself monitors the fundamental red lines. If there is any deviation, if there is any misuse, the practice of calling ministers to committees and holding them accountable has also been established, so there are sufficient checks and balances systems within this system. The role of the parliament is especially expected to hold the government accountable and responsible by utilizing these to the fullest.
Regarding the Dalit Women Commission, etc., these ceilings were set before we arrived. We hope that this year we have set very ambitious revenue targets. We have set a target of 7 percent annual economic growth to make the economy dynamic. This means that the economy, which is currently 66 trillion, will reach about 74 trillion as we manage it. Accordingly, if the state's treasury also increases slightly, I also wish that more than average allocations can be made to these constitutional commissions next year. But I would like to remind them that the ceilings were set on February 15, before we came on March 13 after the February 21 elections, during the time of the previous government. Therefore, this year our room for maneuver was very limited. But if we can increase the fiscal space, we have the desire to further strengthen these very important commissions in accordance with the spirit of the constitution next year. But this is not just about allocating funds in the name of budget allocation. If the concerned commissions bring flagship programs, it will be easier for us to allocate accordingly. Even this time, if these concerned commissions had requested special funds for our special projects, we had time until the end of Baishakh to address them. But since such requests did not come, I want to inform the respected house about what happened this time.
Honorable Shah has stated that the authority given by this parliament is being misused, political prejudice is being shown, etc. It seems you are quoting past practices. We came to form this government on March 13. We have not gone in that direction. Rather, I have cut the discretionary power of the Ministry of Finance in many matters, including budget reallocation, and given it to the concerned ministries. The system of having to go to the Ministry of Finance for months by shuffling files has been reduced within a month of my arrival. This is for capital expenditure, and for the concerned ministry to spend the allocated amount, we have made unprecedented empowerment for that. After the Ministry of Finance brings the budget, it should monitor the implementation and its quality. But we have changed the image of the Ministry of Finance, which used to give approval by heading and had the image of a powerful ministry, and I want to inform you that work will be done differently this year.
Now, regarding the imposition of taxes on education, health, electricity, and the killing of the poor, I have already clarified this for the eighth time. But the honorable members either did not listen or did not understand, or I could not explain. It is not like that. In education, almost three-fourths of permanent Nepali children go to public schools. Only about 24 percent go to private schools, and many of you here have come into politics with socialist principles, or from the influence of communist politics. On the very first day, the principle of reciprocity will be taught to all of you. In accordance with the principle of progressivism, this is a progressive tax brought according to the principle of giving from those who can to those who cannot. For the middle class and upper class who send their children to private schools. When those who pay an average tuition fee of 8,000, 10,000 rupees pay 200-300 rupees, this is a fee used to improve the public education system, which will go to the Dalit families of Dailekh, the marginalized families of Jumla. The political party CPN (Maoist) which came after long and arduous struggle and sacrifice in 2064 BS also started this. But why was this done at that time, it was ignored...

It could not be done, or later this reduction continued. But it is necessary. This is a fee brought to address our majority poor class. Then what about the middle class? Are we killing the middle class? Is it that we are burning the middle class? That is also not the case. This year, we have taken a revolutionary step by making income tax zero up to 1 million rupees for the middle class. The middle class must be given relief. In the current situation where aggregate demand has collapsed, we need to make the market dynamic. We have brought unprecedented tax cut programs this year, saying that disposable income must be increased. Income tax is zero from 400,000 rupees up to 1 million rupees at once, and middle-class parents who send their children to private schools can also get a deduction of up to 25,000 rupees for expenses incurred on education. Therefore, this should be done very thoughtfully so that it reaches the poor class. We need to make major reforms in the educational system accessible to the poor class. We will also arrange funds for that. Even now, we spend about 220 trillion rupees in the education sector. But for those accessed by the middle class, relief has also been provided by allowing deductions on income tax and education expenses. Therefore, if the honorable members understand this a little and understand what it is brought for and how it is brought, it will be easier for the discussion. Talks were also held regarding electricity. We have been providing tax exemptions worth tens of billions on electricity for the past 10-14 years, and significant investment has been made. Today, the private sector produces 80 percent of the electricity. Due to the financial incentives provided by the state, the country, which had only 262 megawatts of installed capacity when the Panchayat fell, now has nearly 4300 megawatts, and by the end of this fiscal year, we will have about 5200 megawatts of installed capacity in electricity. One reason for this rise is the encouragement given by the state, and now in the structure of our gross domestic product, we call them utilities, such as drinking water, electricity, and waste management. As urbanization progresses and our per capita income increases, the composition in GDP will also increase. Therefore, these sectors were not previously in the tax net. This sector, which receives so many facilities, and our agriculture-based country, has now shrunk to only 24 percent. Now these electricity sectors will increase from 4, 4, 6 percent. This sector has not been touched by tax. There is another challenge to formalize this sector of the economy. Currently, about 50 percent of our economy, which we call the 66 trillion rupee economy, is outside, informal. Therefore, a policy that this government has brought with great foresight is to reduce this informality. Let the state recognize it. It needs to be gradually brought into the tax net. But while bringing it into the tax net, so that it does not burden the general citizens and consumers, we have said that we will impose a 5 percent VAT on electricity, let the state recognize it and bring it into the tax net in a formalized manner. But let's not touch it up to 50 units, let's give it for free. Then, even if it is 4 percent, the effective rate will be only 3-4 percent. So that it does not burden the consumer, we will adjust the price, the VAT will be visible on the bill, but the consumer will not have to pay this additional amount on the bill, and we will start working from the 1st of Shrawan, and if we cannot do that, we will increase the threshold of 50 units to 100, 150, as much as possible. So why the fuss? Why are we facing so much confusion and criticism as if tax has been imposed when it has not burdened the consumer? The Finance Minister has to do what is in the long-term interest of the country. Even if it seems unpleasant and unpopular at first glance, this government, which has a huge mandate, has to do these things for the good of the country. I have initiated major reforms this year that weak governments would never dare to undertake or accomplish, because if a strong government like this does not dare, no one else will. This has been done. But while doing so, to ensure that the general public is not burdened, education has also been addressed in the same way. Here it is tightened, there it is loosened. In electricity too, here it is tightened, steps have been taken to build a system, to strengthen the system, but so that the consumer is not burdened, especially in the current inflationary environment, so that there is no additional burden, these policies have been brought in a very creative and innovative way. I urge the honorable members to understand it in the same way. There are also light comments being heard, such as taking loans to prepare the budget, etc. This year we are taking loans of about 650 billion rupees. But loans should not be understood in absolute terms. Loans must be understood in relation to the size of the economy. In English, it is called debt. We should not just look at debt, but the debt-to-GDP ratio, that ratio. Even though we are taking domestic and foreign loans of 650 billion rupees this year, the debt-to-GDP ratio will remain the same as it is now. Now, how did this happen? How is this miracle possible? It is because a large amount of the loans we are taking is for old debts. A large portion, about half, of the loans previously taken by the state, by previous governments, will go towards repaying them. We are raising 410 billion rupees in domestic loans. But about 247 billion rupees of that will go towards repaying old debts. We are taking foreign loans of about 247 billion rupees. 72 billion rupees will go towards repaying old debts. The remaining amount will be used to increase the size of the economy, for economic growth. Therefore, even if the debt increases slightly, the size of the economy also increases. If we can increase it from 66 trillion to 74 trillion rupees, our goal is to keep the debt-to-GDP ratio stable at its current level. Therefore, if the honorable members understand, it is understood in relation to the size of the economy. However, if this ratio increases significantly, our federal parliament will definitely take interest, and the government must be held accountable. For example, during the 2015 earthquake, our debt-to-GDP ratio was only 24 percent. But in just seven or eight years, that 24 percent debt-to-GDP ratio has reached 43-44 percent. We are currently around that level. It increased by 18 percentage points in just 6-7 years. Where did that increased debt go? What was its utility? How was the efficiency of allocation? Whether it helped increase the size of the economy or not, these are matters that the honorable house should take interest in, monitor, and seek accountability for. If our government also goes in that direction in an unrestrained, irresponsible manner, we expect that the National Assembly and the House of Representatives will definitely hold us accountable. Honorable member Roshni Mechhe said that the tax rates were changed in the Appropriation Bill. That understanding is incorrect. Tax matters do not come in the Appropriation Bill. The Appropriation Bill deals with appropriations. It deals with how to allocate 2924 billion rupees and the legal provisions that come with it. It seemed to me that the honorable member picked up on the negative rumors and propaganda spread in the market. The tax rates did not change after the honorable members received the booklet of the Finance Bill. The Finance Minister is supposed to change the tax rates on the morning of Jestha 15th, that is his job. This time, after 2048 BS, we have made significant structural reforms in four tax areas at once, making them industry-friendly, private sector-friendly, and stimulating the economy by making major structural reforms in income tax, value-added tax, customs duties, and excise duties. To encourage domestic production and to eliminate past anomalies with a single blow, the customs duties on finished products were kept lower than those on raw materials for dozens of items. Such distorted practices were carried out to prevent industrialization in this country. I have corrected that this time, and in the process of making that reform, we have consolidated excise duty, VAT, income tax, customs duties, and green taxes in the Finance Bill, making a great effort for such a major reform in a short time. Accordingly, the tax was adjusted and reformed, and the budget speech was delivered on Jestha 15th. It is finalized only on the morning of Jestha 15th. While going through that process, some minor errors in one or two rates were made by the staff. Before the honorable members received the booklet, I wrote a letter to the Secretary-General of Parliament stating that there were some minor errors. Before the honorable members received it, I asked them to provide a page stating that these things have been corrected in the draft of the Finance Bill. Therefore, not a single dot, not a single full stop, not a single letter, not a single comma has been changed in the Finance Bill. Therefore, I earnestly request that the politics of slander, such as repeatedly changing tax rates, doing it for so-and-so, and doing that, should not arise, at least in the National Assembly. Regarding federalism, it is also said that less money went to federalism, etc. It would be easier if you spoke with facts. This year, the equalization grants to local and provincial levels have increased. It would be easier if the honorable members presented the facts. It has increased, not decreased. For some years now, there has been a practice where projects desired by the center are implemented through provinces and local levels, but programs desired by the center are imposed. We will improve this. We will improve this. This time, due to time constraints, as I mentioned earlier. 80 percent of the budget was prepared before the government was formed. Regular work had already been set. With a ceiling of 1890 billion rupees, many programs had already been decided, so it was not possible to expand it. If the commission's proposal came earlier, we could have given 10 billion rupees if it asked for 10 billion rupees. But what would it be spent on? How would it be done? Is there the capacity for that? The capacity of the state is being questioned here. When only 35 percent of the capital expenditure of 407 billion rupees has been spent even on the 15th of Asar, with only two weeks left, only 35 percent of the capital expenditure has been spent. Therefore, the limitations of the state's capacity are on one side. On the other hand, our desires are unlimited, but spending happens only when money comes. If we have the capacity to spend along with the novelty of the program, we can do many things, I would like to place this before you. Honorable Narayan Dutt Bhat raised the issue that a large budget has come and a lot has been spent. As I said regarding loans, the size of the budget must also be considered in relation to the size of the economy. If I tell the honorable members that I have brought a budget of 60 trillion rupees, what will the honorable members think? Is it less or more? With what benchmark should it be measured? We should always measure these figures in relation to the size of the economy to have some relevance. 21 trillion is a ratio within the 66 trillion economy. But as this budget is being spent, how much have we projected? We have projected an economy of 74 trillion rupees. Therefore, the size of the announced budget is only 28.5 percent of the projected size of the economy. This is the smallest, most disciplined budget in the last 12 years. Therefore, honorable members should not speak based on hearsay that a large budget has come, it will not be implemented, it is like a balloon. The size of the budget is 2124 billion rupees. The projected size of the economy is 7458 billion rupees. Divide

We will do it. Every phone also has a calculator. The budget is 28 percent, the smallest budget in the last 12 years. We are trying to bind ourselves with discipline. A government with such a huge majority could have brought a budget with great freedom, couldn't it? By binding ourselves, because we do not want to betray the country. We want to be responsible. We want to lay the foundation this year. We want to gain momentum in the second and third years. In the fourth and fifth years, we want to share the benefits gained from this strategy with the general Nepali public. We want to share the dividends of that development. We have come with this foresight, and this is not new. If the honorable members take the trouble to read the theoretical basis of the Rastriya Swatantra Party, the manifesto we wrote, the 100-point governance reform we formulated, the policy and program we brought, and the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill, they will find unprecedented progress. We are doing what we said we would do. I have also covered the points raised by other honorable members, Vishnu Kumari Sapkota and Honorable Somnath. Finally, there are also issues of education and health. I have already mentioned them. I clarified education earlier, and I clarified electricity. In health, this time we have taken a program to provide nutritious food of Rs 1,000 per month to 313,000 Dalit children across the country, incurring an additional liability of approximately Rs 4 billion. In health, you spend small amounts in private hospitals, lakhs of rupees. I said earlier that 3 percent means if you spend Rs 10,000 on treatment or education, it is Rs 300. That amount is directly spent on nutritious food for a child from a disaster-stricken family in Jajarkot, a Dalit and marginalized family, and for children from all other backgrounds in 25 districts with low human development index and 24 districts. We have talked about inclusivity, we have talked about a society oriented towards equality. Are these basic things now being opposed elsewhere, or are they being directed here, or perhaps to deceive the public by saying that taxes and fees have been increased, this voice has also been raised in the press and in the House of Representatives? But in the National Assembly, the filtered honorable members will provide a certain level. Because it is expected from you, and it goes directly to health and nutrition programs. We are spending about 9 billion rupees. A few billion rupees will be collected from this fee. It will be a partial support, and the goal is to strengthen the health system of the entire country. This year, we are spending about 1 kharba on health and nutrition. We are spending 95 arba. Last year, 10 billion rupees were allocated for health insurance. I have added another 10 billion rupees only after I came. All this belongs to the common Nepali people! And that money doesn't come from the sky. If we only spend and distribute so much, we will be in the state of Zimbabwe and Venezuela. We also need to find sources, and the strategy we have adopted is that when the informal sector is so large in terms of income, it is difficult to increase income tax, but since consumption is widespread, we need to raise funds by imposing small taxes on consumption, even if it's drop by drop. We need to raise 1580 billion rupees. And at this juncture, if we don't impose taxes and don't raise loans, how will it run? Therefore, this is a very restrained, disciplined budget brought with extreme foresight. There may be areas that need improvement. We also didn't have time this time. It is a budget prepared in just four weeks, this is a historic budget. I think we can come with a longer time and thorough preparation for next year's budget. We can address many programs and ideas that honorable members feel were missed this year and bring an even better, superior budget next year than this year. With the hope that we will have the goodwill and cooperation of the honorable members, I conclude. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable members, the discussion on the proposal 'Be it resolved that the Appropriation Bill, 2083 be considered' received with a message from the House of Representatives is hereby concluded. Honorable members, I now present the proposal for decision, 'Be it resolved that the Appropriation Bill, 2083 be considered' received with a message from the House of Representatives. Honorable members in favor of this proposal will say 'Aye' and honorable members against this proposal will say 'Nay'. Honorable members in favor of this proposal will say 'Aye'. - 'Aye'. Honorable members against this proposal will say 'Nay'. - 'Nay'. Since the majority of honorable members are in favor of 'Aye', I declare that the proposal 'Be it resolved that the Appropriation Bill, 2083 be considered' received with a message from the House of Representatives has been approved by a majority. Honorable members, regarding the Appropriation Bill, 2083 received with a message from the House of Representatives, I would like to inform the honorable members who wish to give notice of a proposal for reduction of expenditure that they can submit their notice to the legislative branch of the National Assembly in accordance with Rule 136 of the National Assembly Regulations, 2075. Honorable members, I have set the dates for discussion on various titles of the Appropriation Bill, 2083 received with a message from the House of Representatives as Ashadh 18 and 19, 2083, and the dates for responses from the relevant ministers as Ashadh 22 and 23, 2083. Honorable members who wish to participate in the discussion should provide their names on a party basis to the Business Section of the National Assembly one day before the discussion. Honorable members, the next meeting of the National Assembly will be held on Wednesday, Ashadh 17, 2083, at 1:15 PM, and this meeting is hereby adjourned. (Thereafter, the meeting was adjourned to be held on Wednesday, Ashadh 17, 2083, at 1:15 PM.) Adjourned: 03:31 PM.

sections.name: Opening
sections.summary_en: The second meeting of the National Assembly commenced at 1:43 PM under the chairmanship of Honorable Narayan Prasad Dahal. The Chairperson invited the Finance Minister to present the Appropriation Bill, 2083.

speakers.name: Narayan Prasad Dahal
speakers.topic: Opening the meeting and inviting Finance Minister

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The theoretical discussion on the Appropriation Bill, 2083 began. Members raised concerns about fiscal transfers, the ambiguity of legal compliance in appropriations, budget allocations for constitutional commissions, the bill's impact on different economic classes, and the lack of coordination and implementation strategies.

speakers.name: Padam Bahadur Pariyar
speakers.topic: Fiscal transfers, legal ambiguity, commission budgets

speakers.name: Madan Kumari Shah "Garima"
speakers.topic: Budget misuse, class impact, implementation capacity

speakers.name: Roshni Mechhe
speakers.topic: Tax rate changes, investment, federalism budget

speakers.name: Narayan Dutt Mishra
speakers.topic: Directionless budget, fiscal risk, implementation issues

key_issues: Impact on middle and poor classes

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Honorable member Somnath Purtal discussed the Appropriation Bill, highlighting concerns about decreasing grants to local levels and provinces, and the concentration of programs at the ministry level. Honorable member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota also discussed the budget, noting issues with equalization grants and revenue sharing, and the need for more focus on agriculture, education, and health.

speakers.name: Somnath Purtal
speakers.topic: Appropriation Bill, federalism, local government funding

speakers.name: Bishnu Kumari Sapkota
speakers.topic: Budget, equalization grants, revenue sharing, agriculture, education, health

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle responded to concerns about intergovernmental fiscal transfers, revenue collection, and delegated authority. He explained the principles of revenue sharing, the role of the Finance Commission, and the government's efforts to empower ministries and ensure accountability. He also addressed the progressive tax on education and health, emphasizing its role in supporting public education.

speakers.name: Dr. Swarnim Wagle
speakers.topic: Fiscal transfers, revenue sharing, delegated authority, progressive taxation

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker discusses tax policies, particularly focusing on relief for the middle and poor classes, and reforms in the electricity sector. They explain the rationale behind tax adjustments, emphasizing the need for economic formalization and state revenue generation while minimizing consumer burden. The speaker also addresses concerns about government debt and budget size, contextualizing them within the overall economy.

speakers.name: Honorable Member
speakers.topic: Tax policies, economic reforms, government debt, budget analysis

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker clarifies misunderstandings regarding changes in tax rates within the Appropriation Bill, explaining that tax adjustments are part of the Finance Bill and are finalized on Jestha 15th. They highlight significant structural reforms in income tax, VAT, customs, and excise duties aimed at promoting domestic production and correcting past anomalies. The speaker also addresses concerns about federalism funding, noting an increase in equalization grants to local and provincial levels.

speakers.name: Honorable Member
speakers.topic: Clarification on tax rate changes, economic reforms, federalism funding

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The speaker refutes claims of a large and unmanageable budget, explaining that the budget size must be assessed relative to the economy's projected size. They state that the current budget is the smallest and most disciplined in 12 years, representing only 28.5% of the projected economy. The speaker also touches upon the limited capacity for capital expenditure, with only 35% spent by mid-Asar, indicating a need for improved state capacity and program novelty.

speakers.name: Honorable Member
speakers.topic: Budget size analysis, economic projections, government spending capacity

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The discussion on the Appropriation Bill, 2083 concluded, and the bill was approved by a majority vote. The National Assembly also set dates for further discussions and responses from ministers regarding the bill. Notices for expenditure reduction proposals were also invited.

speakers.name: Honorable Chairperson
speakers.topic: Concluding discussion and presenting bill for vote

sections.name: Adjournment
sections.summary_en: The National Assembly announced the schedule for the next meeting, which will take place on Ashadh 17, 2083, at 1:15 PM. The current meeting was then adjourned.

title: Complete Proceedings of the Twenty-First Session – 15 Asar 2083 Monday (Meeting No. 22)
